papers.title_in_file: Strategies for running the QAOA at hundreds of qubits
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of QAOA for MaxCut on random 3-regular graphs up to 512 vertices, using instance-independent tree parameters and a Goemans-Williamson warm start.

quotes: Our numerics on random instances do not provide general performance guarantees but do provide substantial evidence
Our results are numerical and we do not offer proofs of performance.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in the abstract and in Section 1.

existing.note: The 512-vertex bound is stated in Section 6 and Section 1/5, not in the abstract, which says up to a few hundred vertices. The classical computation of the expected cut is stated in the abstract; the Section 6 sentence about 3-regular graphs and 512 vertices is verbatim.
quotes: We restrict our attention to MaxCut on 3-regular graphs and on problem sizes of up to 512 vertices.
For each instance studied, we classically compute the expected size of the QAOA distribution of cuts; producing the actual cuts requires running on a quantum computer.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 6 and the abstract state the paper's own scope.

existing.note: The paper's full-Hilbert-space data (sizes 20, 24, 28) all lie above the conjectured bound, but for bipartite graphs the paper states that at large size the approximation ratios will lie on the bound, not beyond it. 'Well beyond' holds for the random 3-regular graphs; the bipartite case is the limiting exception, and the large-n statements are expectations, not measurements.
existing.value: The authors report that in their numerical study of random 3-regular graphs at sizes 20, 24 and 28 all of the data lie above the fixed angle conjecture bound, and they state that for bipartite 3-regular graphs the approximation ratios will, for large n, lie on the bound.

assertions.value: The paper states the Fixed Angle Conjecture of Wurtz and Love: the depth-p QAOA at the optimal tree parameters has, for any graph in the family of D-regular graphs of all sizes, an approximation ratio at least as great as the optimal value of the tree central-edge expectation.

assertions.value: The authors propose a procedure of classically determining the optimal parameters for the cost function on the central edge of a 3-regular tree of radius p, as a one-shot calculation whose parameters will be used for all instances of any size at this value of p, with two strategies: standard QAOA at the tree parameters, or the modified GW warm-start QAOA at the tree parameters, each optionally followed by a parameter search.
quotes: Consider a 3-regular tree with radius p.
Classically determine the optimal parameters (γ∗, β∗) for the cost function on the central edge.
This is a one-shot calculation, and the parameters (γ∗, β∗) will be used for all instances of any size at this value of p.
Hardware resources permitting, use the parameters (γ∗, β∗) as the starting point of a parameter
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposed procedure; the claim that the parameters serve all sizes is supported only by the numerics up to 512 vertices and p = 5.
assertions.reader_inference: The one-shot claim for 'any size' goes beyond the sizes tested (up to 512 vertices) and depths (up to p = 5 on large graphs).

assertions.value: The authors state that using tree parameters as the initial point of a variational optimization typically gives only slight improvements and results comparable to a full optimization, which suggests that in practice the QAOA can achieve near-optimal performance without parameter optimization.
quotes: Further, by using tree parameters as the initial point of a variational optimization, we typically see only slight improvements and get results comparable to performing a full optimization.
This suggests that in practice, the QAOA can achieve near-optimal performance without the need for parameter optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from numerics on one ensemble.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion is limited by the paper's own scope: random 3-regular graphs, up to 512 vertices, and p up to 5 on the large graphs.
